offers.message: Proposing a 1-for-1 swap: Mega Charizard Y (20) for Mega Floette (20). Mega Charizard Y's mega stone has been expended and it can no longer mega-evolve, leaving a dead slot on my roster. Mega Floette brings powerful Fairy STAB via Moonblast, Flower Veil to block status on allies in doubles, and Symbiosis for creative item support. At 20 points each, the trade keeps both rosters at budget.
offers.offerReasoning: Mega Charizard Y is expended and unusable in future games, creating a critical dead slot on a 10-Pokemon roster. Sun has been consistently shut down by Cloud Nine and Sand Stream across all three matches, so pivoting away from sun dependency is essential. Mega Floette fills the slot with a usable Pokemon whose Fairy STAB (Moonblast) pressures Dragons and Dark types, Flower Veil provides doubles support, and Symbiosis enables item-passing strategies. Hazard removal remains the top priority for the next trade phase.
offers.responseReasoning: With its Mega Stone expended, Charizard Y effectively becomes a much weaker base Charizard and would overlap heavily with Talonflame’s Fire/Flying role. Mega Floette is a premier special Fairy with 155 SpA, 148 SpD, 102 Speed, and Fairy Aura, so trading it for an unusable mega slot is a substantial downgrade.

offers.offerReasoning: No trade is sufficiently attractive at mid-season. The roster is already budget-maxed, so most upgrades would require an equal-cost exchange; the realistic options would sacrifice established tools such as Mamoswine's immediate weather pressure, Farigiraf's anti-priority and speed-control support, or Sneasler's disruption. Retaining the complete roster best preserves flexible matchup-specific sixes for the remaining opponents.

No equal-cost swap presents a clear upgrade over the current role compression. The roster already has distinct Mega Floette and Mega Alakazam modes, Talonflame/Hatterene dual speed control, and Scrafty/Milotic disruption; moving a low-cost glue piece would risk weakening those established lines more than it improves a matchup.

My current roster sits at a clean 100/100 points, featuring a potent rain core anchored by Pelipper, Mega Swampert, Basculegion, and Primarina, alongside supportive and utility pieces like Whimsicott, Alakazam, Forretress, Mega Ampharos, and Feraligatr. Having gone 2-1 and successfully ironing out my rain strategies and anti-rain checks, holding my roster gives me stability as I prepare for the regular season.

offers.message: Straight 1-for-1 swap: I get Altaria for its Ground immunity and Water resist to patch my sand team's biggest holes. In return you get Absol — Sucker Punch, Feint, and Shadow Sneak give you priority that actually works under Trick Room (unlike Altaria's Tailwind which is anti-synergy with your TR setup). Absol also brings Knock Off, Taunt, and Close Combat as fast utility under TR. Clean lateral move for both of us.
offers.offerReasoning: Altaria (Dragon/Flying) is immune to Ground and resists Water — my team's two biggest weaknesses with zero current Ground resists and 4 Water-weak mons. It adds Tailwind speed control, Roost recovery, Will-O-Wisp, and Natural Cure utility. I only lose Absol's niche Sucker Punch priority, which Grimmsnarl's Dark typing already partially covers. Entrant 4 runs TR where Altaria's Tailwind is anti-synergy, making Absol's TR-friendly priority more useful to them.
offers.responseReasoning: Altaria provides the roster’s only Ground immunity, along with valuable Water resistance and Cloud Nine utility against weather, which helps protect Archaludon and Armarouge. Absol’s priority and Taunt are useful, but its poor bulk and limited defensive value make it a much less reliable Trick Room support piece; the claimed priority advantage does not compensate for losing Altaria’s unique resistances and Helping Hand access.

offers.offerReasoning: My 3-0 roster has no exploitable weaknesses and every slot pulls its weight. The only mathematically legal trades (Clawitzer↔Ampharos-Mega at 4pts, or Furfrou↔any 1pt mon) are sidegrades at best. Ampharos-Mega is slow and redundant with Rotom-Wash/Dragapult; no 1-point free agent or owned mon matches Furfrou's Fur Coat utility. Both remaining opponents (Sun and Sand+Shadow Tag) are already well-covered by my existing anti-sun core and Dragapult/Rotom-Wash respectively.

decisions.reasoning: Dropping the entire sun core (Charizard-Mega Y, Venusaur) and low-value Heracross to pivot away from sun offense, which lost all three games. Glimmora provides automatic Toxic Spikes via Toxic Debris plus Stealth Rock/Spikes/Corrosion for Gholdengo coverage. Mimikyu's Disguise + Swords Dance + Play Rough gives a non-sun win condition and a direct Fairy-type answer to Gholdengo. Palafin's Zero to Hero + Jet Punch priority is a powerful rain/sand-neutral threat that doesn't depend on weather. Skarmory stays for Defog, keeping hazard control intact. Budget: 13+11+12=36 added, 20+13+3=36 dropped.

I am making no trades. The current roster already preserves the Archaludon/Mamoswine/Armarouge offensive shell, Altaria's Cloud Nine and Tailwind, and the supporting tools needed for redirection, recovery, disruption, Nuzzle, and speed-control denial. No available free agent improves the Rotom-Wash, Mega Gengar, sun, and sand matchups broadly enough to justify sacrificing one of these established roles.

The current 100-point roster already has distinct, matchup-relevant modes: Mega Floette endgames, Life Orb Garchomp pressure, Talonflame Tailwind, Hatterene Trick Room, and Mega Alakazam speed offense. No available free agent improves those roles enough to justify losing the established anti-sand, anti-rain, and anti-Metagross coverage supplied by the current ten.

Sitting at 3rd place with a 2-1 record and a strong, fully-synergized rain core (Pelipper, Mega Swampert, Basculegion, Primarina, Whimsicott), our roster is already at the 100/100 budget cap and performing excellently. Our series reflections and wins highlight that our current team handles physical pivots and defensive archetypes with ease, so keeping our current roster intact for the regular season is our best path forward.

Three targeted upgrades: Hydrapple replaces Chandelure with a Water/Ground-resistant Regenerator pivot (Giga Drain 4x SE on Swampert-Mega, Earth Power 2x SE on Metagross-Mega) — critical for the rain matchup while still hitting Steel types. Houndoom replaces the dead-weight Absol at equal cost with Dark/Fire typing, Flash Fire immunity, and Flamethrower/Heat Wave coverage (2x SE on Klefki). Rotom replaces Sandaconda with Levitate Ground immunity — the team's biggest structural hole — while adding Electric STAB (4x SE on Pelipper) and Ghost typing for the spam core.

The 3-0 roster is balanced, type-diverse, and has verified answers for both remaining opponents. Furfrou's Ghost immunity is specifically valuable into Mega Gengar (Week 5), and no 1-point alternative offers comparable role compression. Clawitzer's Mega Launcher-boosted special Water offense fills a unique niche that Rotom-Wash's defensive pivot set doesn't cover. Standing pat preserves proven synergy.

seasonReviews.outcome: You finished 6th of 6 in the round robin and missed the playoffs. Your season is over.
seasonReviews.summary: The season was a 0-5, 0-10 last-place finish. The initial sun core built around 20-point Mega Charizard Y was consistently shut down by Cloud Nine and Sand Stream, and even after a mid-season pivot to a weather-neutral roster featuring Palafin, Mimikyu, and Glimmora, the team failed to win a single game across all five series.
seasonReviews.didWell: The mid-season trade window pivot was the right macro decision — correctly identifying that sun was unrecoverable and swapping to Glimmora, Mimikyu, and Palafin gave the team new win conditions and type coverage. Several draft picks held up well regardless: Toxapex at 8 points was excellent value as a Regenerator pivot, Aegislash at 14 was a versatile Ghost/Steel answer to many meta threats, Skarmory at 3 was nearly free hazard control and Defog, and Swampert at 6 cleanly provided the Ground immunity the team desperately needed. The post-FAM roster construction on paper was reasonable with layered hazard pressure, priority, and dedicated Fairy and Psychic checks.
seasonReviews.didPoorly: The 20-point Mega Charizard Y pick was the defining mistake — it consumed a quarter of the budget and locked the entire team into a sun strategy that was countered in week 1 and never became viable again. Venusaur at 13 points was a second dead investment in Chlorophyll speed that meant nothing without reliable sun. Torkoal at 15 points was expensive dead weight once Charizardite Y was expended and Drought became unreliable. Heracross at 3 points was filler that was immediately dropped at the trade window. The result was a 0-10 record — the post-FAM roster looked competent on paper but never translated into a single win, suggesting the remaining budget was too thin or the six selected each week were still exploitable.
seasonReviews.wouldChange: First, never take Mega Charizard Y at 20 — spend those points on a pick that contributes in non-sun games rather than one that becomes a dead slot the moment its mega stone is used. Second, drop Venusaur entirely and reallocate those 13 points toward a second reliable win condition or a deeper defensive backbone. Third, keep Torkoal only if paired with a plan that doesn't rely on Drought — or replace it with a cheaper pivot and spend the saved 15 points on the remaining slots. Fourth, after pivoting at the trade window, the team needed at least one more high-impact pick rather than three mid-tier ones; the 3-point Heracross drop should have been replaced with something that addressed the post-FAM team's still-thin offensive firepower.

seasonReviews.outcome: You finished 5th of 6 in the round robin and missed the playoffs. Your season is over.
seasonReviews.summary: I finished 2-3 and missed playoffs because the roster had a strong weather-and-Trick-Room shell but no dependable answers to several central defensive and disruption problems. The two wins showed the team could execute its intended plan, while the three losses exposed both draft-window gaps and avoidable registration and piloting mistakes.
seasonReviews.didWell: Archaludon, Farigiraf, Sinistcha, Sneasler, Armarouge, and Mamoswine gave me a genuinely flexible core, and Altaria was an excellent one-point pick: Cloud Nine and Tailwind directly enabled the 2-0 win over the sun team and the 2-0 win over the rain team. The Week 1 registration correctly paired Altaria with Mamoswine and Armarouge, and the Week 4 registration used Freeze-Dry, Thunderbolt, Fake Out, and redirection to attack the opponent's actual rain structure rather than forcing Trick Room. Declining Absol itself was defensible because Altaria's Ground immunity, Cloud Nine, and Tailwind were uniquely valuable, and I correctly identified Rotom-Wash and Mega Gengar as problems after facing them.
seasonReviews.didPoorly: The draft left me without a reliable Rotom-Wash or Milotic answer and without a robust anti-Mega-Gengar route; those were draft weaknesses, not problems that every possible registration could have solved. At the window, I overvalued preserving the roster: I made no coach offer, declined the only incoming Absol swap, and made no free-agent change even after the first three weeks had revealed exactly these structural holes. Week 3 was primarily a piloting and registration failure: despite knowing Mega Gengar used Taunt and Protect to stall Trick Room, I brought a six centered on Farigiraf's Trick Room and never established a credible non-Trick-Room plan. Week 5 repeated the issue against Milotic and Mega Alakazam, registering passive or unreliable pressure into Recover and Icy Wind while relying on a Choice Scarf Sneasler whose Unburden plan was inactive and leaving myself without a convincing late-game answer.
seasonReviews.wouldChange: At the draft, I would spend one of the expensive support slots on a direct Rotom-Wash/Milotic answer rather than accepting three overlapping speed-control and support options around Archaludon. At the trade window, I would actively pursue a replacement for either Altaria or a redundant support slot only if it produced concrete Electric-, Grass-, or anti-Gengar coverage; if Absol remained the only offer, I would still decline it, but I would not automatically keep all ten unchanged. Against GLM in Week 3, I would register a fast, non-Trick-Room six with Sneasler and Dedenne pressure, preserve Armarouge's Wide Guard, and treat Farigiraf as optional rather than making Taunt-and-Protect Gengar fight my primary mode. Against Terra in Week 5, I would prioritize a way to deny Milotic's Recover or remove it quickly, bring a more coherent Mega Alakazam answer, and avoid the Scarf Sneasler set unless its speed benchmarks and role were demonstrably better than a normal offensive or utility set.

seasonReviews.outcome: You reached the playoffs as the 4th seed and were eliminated in the semifinals. Your season is over.
seasonReviews.summary: We finished 4th in the regular season at 3-2 and reached the semifinals, where our 0-2 loss to deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro ended our run. While our rain core dominated favorable matchups, structural vulnerabilities to Grass-types like Serperior and weather disruption capped our ceiling.
seasonReviews.didWell: We drafted an exceptionally cohesive rain archetype early, locking down elite offensive powerhouses like Pelipper, Mega Swampert, and Basculegion-Male alongside premium support in Whimsicott and Primarina. This core steamrolled sun and sand teams cleanly, securing solid 2-0 and 2-1 victories against inclusionai/ring-2.6-1t and z-ai/glm-5.2.
seasonReviews.didPoorly: Our draft bench suffered from wasted depth and random fallback picks, leaving us with unplayable roster slots like Castform and underutilized threats like Feraligatr and Alakazam instead of essential anti-grass or anti-dragon defensive pivots. Piloting a linear rain strategy also left us helpless against dedicated counter-picks like deepseek's Serperior and Rotom-Wash cores.
seasonReviews.wouldChange: Draft a diverse defensive backup instead of wasting points on filler Pokémon like Castform and redundant water types like Feraligatr. Bring tailored anti-grass and electric checks like an Amoonguss or a Dragonite rather than relying purely on linear Swift Swim offense. Actively utilize the mid-season trade window to patch our glaring Serperior and Rotom-Wash weaknesses instead of keeping an unadjusted roster.

seasonReviews.outcome: You reached the playoffs as the 2nd seed and were eliminated in the semifinals. Your season is over.
seasonReviews.summary: I finished 3-2, earned the second seed, and reached the semifinals before a 0-2 playoff loss to GLM. The season was successful overall, but the elimination exposed that our excellent Mega Floette/Garchomp core did not always translate into a sufficiently durable plan against GLM’s Tyranitar, sand, Mega Gengar, and Gholdengo endgame.
seasonReviews.didWell: The draft was strong: Mega Floette, Garchomp, Milotic, Talonflame, Scrafty, and the 6-point Metagross/Hisui Goodra values gave us real Tailwind, Trick Room, anti-Intimidate, and alternate-Mega modes. The Week 1 2-1 over GLM and Week 4 2-0 over Ring showed that the Garchomp/Scrafty/Talonflame/Floette structure was genuinely effective into sand, Steel, and slower defensive teams; Week 5’s 2-0 also validated registering Mega Alakazam as a matchup-specific anti-Sneasler and anti-Trick Room option. Declining the Mega Floette-for-expended-Mega-Charizard-Y trade was plainly correct, and keeping the roster was defensible because no listed swap replaced Floette’s role or meaningfully improved the rain, sand, and Metagross matchups at once.
seasonReviews.didPoorly: The Week 2 rain loss was primarily a registration and piloting problem: despite bringing Manectric and a Trick Room mode, we still relied too heavily on fragile Hatterene speed control into Pelipper, Waterfall Mega Swampert, and flinch pressure, then failed to preserve Floette consistently for its confirmed Energy Ball Swampert assignment. Week 3 against the eventual first seed was a roster-window result as much as a series loss: Mega Metagross behind Klefki screens, Incineroar, and Rotom-Wash stressed our physical and Ground-centric answers, and no free-agency adjustment was made to sharpen that matchup. The playoff 0-2 to GLM was the clearest registration/piloting failure: we correctly identified Tyranitar’s Crunch, Excadrill’s sash and Sand Rush, Garchomp’s Ice Punch risk, and the Gengar/Gholdengo backline, but still did not produce a durable Tyranitar plan or keep Mega Alakazam and Milotic safe enough to convert their intended roles.
seasonReviews.wouldChange: At the midseason window, I would have actively pursued a swap or free-agent replacement for one of the redundant slow special pivots—most plausibly Hisuian Goodra or Hatterene—to add a more reliable Tyranitar/Gholdengo/Rotom-Wash answer; keeping all ten unchanged was a window decision that left the eventual GLM rematch too similar to Week 1. For the playoff rematch with GLM, I would register Metagross over one of the two Megas or over Talonflame: Clear Body, Bullet Punch, and its Steel resistance give a more stable board piece against Gengar/Gholdengo than an all-in dual-Mega selection. Against rain, I would build the six around a safer Fake Out plus Trick Room line and treat Mega Floette as a protected Swampert check rather than exposing it early, while using Manectric as targeted disruption instead of assuming Lightning Rod alone solves the Water matchup.

seasonReviews.outcome: You won the final. You are the league champion and the season is over.
seasonReviews.summary: Won the championship at 3-2 in regular season (7-4 games) then swept through two playoff rounds, avenging the week 1 loss to terra and edging deepseek 2-1 in the final — the sand core of Tyranitar + Excadrill was the engine that carried every series, and the trade window swaps (Rotom, Houndoom, Hydrapple) patched enough holes to flip the terra rematch.
seasonReviews.didWell: The Tyranitar (14) + Excadrill (13) sand core at 27 combined points was the best value decision of the draft — it appeared in every single series and provided speed control, weather override, and spread Rock Slide pressure that no opponent could fully answer. The trade window was excellent: all three swaps were upgrades that addressed real structural holes, and Houndoom in particular proved its worth as the Metagross-Mega and Dragapult answer against deepseek in both meetings. The playoff adaptation against terra — adding Rotom for Ground immunity and Grimmsnarl with Adamant Spirit Break to threaten Garchomp — showed genuine learning from the week 1 loss, turning a 1-2 defeat into a 2-0 sweep. Mega Gengar's Shadow Tag was used intelligently as a trapping tool rather than a standalone sweeper, and the movepool flexibility (Energy Ball for Rotom-Wash, Icy Wind for speed control, Taunt for setup denial) kept opponents guessing.
seasonReviews.didPoorly: The original budget picks were dead weight: Absol (1 pt) and Sandaconda (2 pts) were never registered in a single series, and Chandelure was dropped before it could contribute meaningfully — three draft slots producing zero games is a real waste even at low cost. Vaporeon (5 pts) was drafted specifically as rain insurance yet was never brought in any series, including the week 5 loss to gemini's rain team where it should have been most valuable — that 5 points was effectively dead cap. The week 5 loss to gemini exposed a structural Water weakness that no registration could cover: four Water-weak Pokémon (Tyranitar 4x, Excadrill 2x, Houndoom 2x, Gholdengo 2x) meant the rain matchup was lost at draft, not at the battle screen. The week 1 loss to terra was partly a piloting issue — the opponent's Protect reads were called out in prep notes yet still punished.
seasonReviews.wouldChange: I would consolidate the three weakest budget picks (Absol 1, Sandaconda 2, Chandelure 6 = 9 points) into one better Pokémon at the draft rather than waiting for the trade window to fix them — a 9-point Water resist like Gyarados or Milotic would have addressed the rain hole from day one. I would cut Vaporeon entirely, since a 5-point mon that never sees a single series is worse than spending those points elsewhere on the roster. I would have pushed harder for the Altaria trade or found another Ground-immune Pokémon before week 5, since the gemini loss was directly caused by having no answer to Swift Swim sweepers under rain-boosted Water STAB. I would have registered Grimmsnarl in week 1 against terra instead of Tauros, since the prep notes identified Scrafty's Snarl spam and Garchomp EQ as the primary threats — Prankster screens and Spirit Break answered both better than Intimidate alone.

seasonReviews.outcome: You reached the final and lost it. You are the league runner-up and your season is over.
seasonReviews.summary: Finished 4-1 in the regular season and reached the playoff final, but lost to the same Sand + Mega Gengar team twice — the one matchup my roster was never built to solve.
seasonReviews.didWell: The Incineroar–Mega Metagross–Dragapult–Rotom-Wash top four was a superb draft core that carried me through rain, sun, Trick Room, and Fairy Aura matchups. Serperior at 5 points was the steal of the draft, single-handedly winning both rain series against Gemini (4-0 in games) with Contrary Leaf Storm snowballs. My game-planning and set registration were sharp: I correctly identified win conditions for each opponent and adjusted sets week to week — the Life Orb Dragapult pivot set in week 2, the Chople Berry Incineroar for Tauros-Aqua in week 4, and the Expert Belt Gliscor for the sun team in week 5 all show strong metagame reading.
seasonReviews.didPoorly: The bottom three draft picks — Gliscor (3 pts), Clawitzer (4 pts), and Furfrou (1 pt) — combined for 8 points and were registered only twice across seven series, contributing almost nothing. The trade-window decision to stand pat at 3-0 was complacent: GLM-5.2 added Houndoom (a Flash Fire Dark-type that blanked my Incineroar and threatened Dragapult), and I made no counter-adjustment despite knowing they were my biggest threat. The Mega Gengar matchup was never adequately solved — Dragapult's Life Orb Shadow Ball was only a 67–152% roll to OHKO, and Shadow Tag hard-countered the entire pivoting identity of my team (Parting Shot, Volt Switch, U-turn), yet I drafted no backup plan beyond a never-used Furfrou.
seasonReviews.wouldChange: Replace the Gliscor–Clawitzer–Furfrou trio at picks 48/49/60 with a dedicated Shadow Tag answer: a Choice Scarf Dark-type like Krookodile or a Sucker Punch user like Kingambit that could reliably remove Mega Gengar without needing to pivot. Use the trade window to add a Fire-immune Dark-type (Houndoom or Flash Fire Chandelure) after seeing GLM-5.2's roster, dropping Clawitzer whose Mega Launcher niche was redundant with Rotom-Wash and Dragapult already covering special offense. Bring Corviknight over Serperior from the first Gengar series — Serperior was dead weight into sand and I learned that lesson in a 0-2 loss that ultimately cost me tiebreaker positioning for the final.

roster.name: Incineroar
roster.rationale: Incineroar is the most role-dense Pokémon in the format: Intimidate cycling, Fake Out pressure, and slow Parting Shot pivoting all on one Fire/Dark chassis. It fits onto virtually any archetype — sun, rain, Trick Room, balance — and its unique combination of disruption and bulk is irreplaceable on this board. At 18 points it's a premium but fair price for the single most proven VGC cornerstone.

roster.name: Mega Metagross
roster.rationale: Mega Metagross (17 pts) is the best Mega still on the board — 80/145/150/105/110/110 with Tough Claws gives both elite bulk and nuclear physical damage. It pairs well with Incineroar: Metagross covers Incineroar's Rock and Fairy weaknesses, while Incineroar's Dark typing handles the Ghost and Dark moves that threaten Metagross. At 110 base Speed it also gives me a fast mode that can set Stealth Rock or go straight offensive, keeping tempo after an Incineroar pivot.

roster.name: Dragapult
roster.rationale: Dragapult (14) fills three urgent needs at once: a blazing-fast special attacker (base 142 Speed, 100 SpA), a Ground immunity via its Ghost typing, and a disruptive support toolkit (Will-O-Wisp, Thunder Wave, screens, U-turn). It pairs beautifully with Incineroar's Intimidate to neuter physical threats and gives me a pivot core that can control tempo. At 14 points it leaves 51 for 7 picks — plenty of budget to chase a dedicated Tailwind setter and a secondary Mega later.

roster.name: Rotom-Wash
roster.rationale: Rotom-Wash is the premier defensive pivot still on the board, giving me a crucial Ground immunity via Levitate that my roster sorely needs. Its Electric/Water typing dominates the emerging rain team (Pelipper, Mega Swampert, Basculegion) and resists sun-boosted Fire from inclusionai's Zard Y, while Volt Switch forms a potent pivoting core with Incineroar's Parting Shot. At 14 points it's excellent value, leaving 37 for 6 picks to round out speed control, a secondary Mega, and a Fairy.

roster.name: Klefki
roster.rationale: Klefki is the last remaining Prankster user with a support movepool this deep — priority Thunder Wave, Reflect, Light Screen, Spikes, and even Trick Room all at +1. Steel/Fairy typing patches my Dark and Dragon weaknesses while stacking beautifully with Incineroar's Intimidate and Rotom-Wash's bulk. At 11 points it leaves 26 for five more picks, keeping a secondary Mega and a dedicated Tailwind setter (Corviknight or Noivern) well within reach.

roster.name: Corviknight
roster.rationale: Corviknight (13) is the ideal Tailwind setter for this roster — a bulky Steel/Flying pivot with Roost, U-turn, and Mirror Armor that adds a crucial Ground immunity alongside Rotom-W's Levitate. It rounds out the defensive core beautifully: Incineroar + Metagross + Rotom-W + Corviknight + Klefki covers each other's weaknesses well, and Tailwind gives Dragapult and Metagross a fast mode beyond Klefki's Thunder Wave/Trick Room. At 13 points it leaves 13 for the final 4 picks, which is tight but workable with budget special attackers like Chandelure (6), Gengar (8), or Gardevoir (10).

roster.name: Serperior
roster.rationale: Serperior (5 pts) fills a critical gap: I have zero Grass coverage against the rain team's Mega Swampert, Basculegion, Feraligatr, and Primarina. Contrary Leaf Storm turns it into a snowball special win condition, 113 base Speed outruns most of the format, and Glare provides speed control that hits Ground-types (unlike Klefki's Thunder Wave). At 5 points it's excellent value, leaving 8 points for my final 3 picks.

roster.name: Gliscor
roster.rationale: Gliscor (3) fills the glaring Ground-type gap in my roster — I currently have zero Ground coverage into Gholdengo, Aegislash, and Archaludon. Poison Heal makes it a status-absorbing defensive pivot that synergises perfectly with my Steel-heavy core (Mega Metagross, Klefki, Corviknight), while its Electric immunity protects Rotom-Wash from Volt Switch spam. At 95 base Speed it outspeeds most defensive mons and can run Toxic/Roost/Earthquake/Protect sets that my bulky offense desperately needs.

roster.name: Clawitzer
roster.rationale: Clawitzer (4 pts) is the ideal special wallbreaker for this roster. Mega Launcher boosts Water Pulse, Dark Pulse, Aura Sphere, and Dragon Pulse to 90–127 BP off 120 base SpA, giving me SE coverage into Steels (Aura Sphere), Ghosts/Dragons (Dark/Dragon Pulse), and Fires (Water Pulse). It also brings Flip Turn for pivoting and rounds out my special attacking core alongside Dragapult and Rotom-Wash. Leaves exactly 1 point for Dedenne as the final pick.

roster.name: Furfrou
roster.rationale: Dedenne is already drafted by Luna-pro, so the private note's plan is void. Furfrou is the best remaining 1-point option: Fur Coat doubles its physical Defense, making it a legitimate bulky pivot at base 102 Speed. It brings Thunder Wave for speed control, U-turn for momentum, and a Ghost immunity that helps against Mega Gengar and Dragapult — unique utility none of the other 1-point leftovers can match.

draftRoster.rationale: Altaria is an excellent one-point utility pick: Cloud Nine directly disrupts both the opposing rain core and the sun roster, while Tailwind, Helping Hand, Haze, and Perish Song give it several viable support modes. Its Dragon/Flying typing also provides a Ground immunity for Archaludon and Sneasler, improving positioning without committing the team to a single speed mode.

draftRoster.name: Meowstic-Female
draftRoster.rationale: Meowstic-Female gives the roster unusually valuable low-cost flexibility: Fake Out, Prankster-independent utility, Trick Room, Helping Hand, dual screens, Thunder Wave, and Yawn. It complements both Farigiraf/Armarouge slower modes and Altaria/Sneasler faster modes while adding a second strong support Psychic without consuming a Mega slot.

draftRoster.name: Qwilfish
draftRoster.rationale: Qwilfish is the best remaining 2-point utility pick: Intimidate adds valuable physical control to a roster that otherwise lacks it, while Water/Poison patches several defensive gaps and gives useful disruption through options such as Taunt, Haze, and Nuzzle. Its decent Speed also lets it function as an active support piece rather than passive Intimidate fodder, and it can pressure the opposing rain core with Poison STAB.

draftRoster.name: Dedenne
draftRoster.rationale: Dedenne is the best remaining 1-point fit, providing fast Nuzzle speed control, Electric/Fairy typing, and useful disruption alongside Qwilfish. Its support utility gives the roster another way to pressure faster teams without competing for the Mega slot or duplicating a major offensive role.

roster.name: Whimsicott
roster.rationale: Securing Whimsicott for 19 points gives us elite Prankster utility, Tailwind setup, and Moonblast offense while leaving us with 81 points for our remaining 9 picks. It pairs exceptionally well with heavy hitters and restricted/mega anchors, and keeps a premier speed-control option out of opponents' hands early in the snake draft.

roster.name: Basculegion-Male
roster.rationale: Since Archaludon was already taken, Basculegion-Male is an elite offensive pivot that thrives under Whimsicott's Prankster Tailwind, threatening massive Adaptability-boosted Wave Slashes and Last Respects in the late game. Its Water/Ghost typing and great offensive stats punish many common switch-ins while immediately applying heavy pressure against early draft cores. This leaves us with 62 points for our remaining 8 picks, leaving ample room for a top-tier Mega evolution and strong defensive/support anchors.

roster.name: Pelipper
roster.rationale: Drafting Pelipper provides automatic Drizzle to power up Basculegion-Male's Water-type attacks and Swift Swim capability, creating an immediate rain archetype core alongside Whimsicott. It also secures a strong weather control option for 18 points, leaving 44 points for 7 remaining picks while preserving flexibility for a premier Mega evolution.

roster.name: Mega Swampert
roster.rationale: With Pelipper establishing permanent rain, Mega Swampert is an elite Swift Swim physical sweeper that abuses the weather and rounds out our offensive core. Its Water/Ground typing and huge 150 Attack stat fit seamlessly alongside our existing rain attackers while keeping our budget healthy. This secures our crucial Mega evolution slot with high synergy.

roster.name: Feraligatr
roster.rationale: Feraligatr is an extremely budget-friendly physical threat (cost: 3) that synergizes well with our Rain core through Sheer Force, boosting moves like Liquidation and Ice Fang. It provides powerful offensive backup without straining our remaining points, leaving us with 26 points for our final 5 picks.

roster.rationale: Primarina provides exceptional defensive utility under rain with its Water/Fairy typing, high Special Defense, and Liquid Voice spread pressure. It covers Dragon and Dark threats while leaving 11 points for our final 4 picks to secure supporting pivots.

teambuilds.rationale: We correct the EV allocations to ensure no stat exceeds 32 Stat Points under the Champions format while keeping our powerful rain core intact. Pelipper sets rain for Mega Swampert and Basculegion, Whimsicott provides fast Prankster support, Primarina acts as a bulky special pivot, and Mega Ampharos breaks through bulky walls with Mold Breaker.

We bring a rain core featuring Pelipper, Mega Swampert, and Basculegion-Male, supported by Whimsicott for Tailwind, Primarina for bulky special offense, and Mega Ampharos to pressure Rotom-Wash, Corviknight, and other defensive pivots. Pelipper sets rain immediately so Mega Swampert and Basculegion can outspeed and overwhelm threats like Mega Metagross and Incineroar under Swift Swim.

This six uses a flexible Trick Room mode through Farigiraf and Armarouge, while Sneasler and the faster investment on Archaludon provide immediate pressure outside Trick Room. Mamoswine targets Mega Metagross, Incineroar, Gliscor, Serperior, and Dragapult, while Armarouge's Wide Guard protects against likely spread attacks and Sinistcha supplies redirection, healing, and sustain. Armor Tail, Fake Out, Taunt, and Helping Hand give the team strong control over the opponent's priority and setup options.

Mega Floette is the primary closer against their Dark-, Water-, and Fighting-type options, while Garchomp supplies immediate pressure into Tyranitar, Excadrill, and Gholdengo. Talonflame Tailwind and Milotic Icy Wind give two ways to deny Mega Gengar and Sand Rush Excadrill their speed advantage; Scrafty disrupts special attackers with Snarl and Intimidate, while Metagross checks Grimmsnarl and can pick off Mega Gengar with Bullet Punch. Favor Talonflame + Metagross or Talonflame + Garchomp leads when early Tailwind is safe, and preserve Floette until their Steel- and Poison-type pressure is contained.

Use Talonflame and Manectric to punish the Pelipper rain lead: priority Tailwind preserves speed control while Lightning Rod can redirect targeted Water- and Electric-type attacks. Mega Floette is the primary breaker, with Energy Ball pressuring Mega Swampert and Fairy Aura-boosted Fairy attacks covering Basculegion, Whimsicott, and Mega Ampharos. Hatterene plus the slow Scrafty/Hisui Goodra core gives a second Trick Room mode that is especially strong into Swift Swim teams.

Cloud Nine Altaria suppresses Mega Charizard Y's sun while setting Tailwind, and Armarouge's Wide Guard protects the team from Heat Wave and other spread attacks. Mamoswine pressures Charizard, Torkoal, Toxapex, Aegislash, and Skarmory with its Ground-, Ice-, and Rock-type coverage, while Archaludon provides strong special damage into the Fire- and Flying-heavy core. Dedenne and Sneasler add speed control, disruption, Fake Out, Quick Guard, and Helping Hand support for flexible four-Pokémon selections.

The opponent's scariest archetype is sun (Mega Charizard Y + Torkoal + Chlorophyll Venusaur), so Tyranitar's Sand Stream is the backbone — it overrides Drought, neuters Fire damage, and activates Excadrill's Sand Rush for a sweeper that outspeeds the entire format. Mega Gengar at 200 Speed outspeeds max Jolly Meowscarada and likely OHKOs with Sludge Bomb, while Shadow Tag traps Toxapex/Aegislash for cleanup. Grimmsnarl provides Prankster screens + Fake Out for safe leads, and Spirit Break is the team's only SE hit into Spiritomb while softening Charizard Y's SpA. Tauros-Aqua brings Intimidate, Water STAB to delete the Fire types, and a Fighting resist to wall Heracross. Gholdengo rounds out with Steel/Ghost typing (resists Grass/Poison/Bug, immune to Fighting), Make It Rain spread damage, and Good as Gold to block status — but must stay away from Charizard Y until sand is firmly set.

The opponent's two Mega options define the matchup: Mega Floette (Fairy Aura Moonblast at 102 Spe) and Mega Alakazam (175 SpA at 150 Spe, Trace). I bring the Sand core (Tyranitar + Excadrill) for speed control—Excadrill at 308 in sand outspeeds everything—plus Gholdengo as the defensive anchor resisting Fairy, Psychic, and Dragon simultaneously. Mega Gengar traps and eliminates weakened targets with Shadow Tag while resisting Fairy. Grimmsnarl provides Prankster screens and Spirit Break to neuter special attackers. Tauros rounds out with Intimidate and 4x-effective Close Combat on Hisuian Goodra. Key defensive wins: Tyranitar is immune to Psychic (hard-walls Alakazam), Gholdengo tanks Floette's Moonblast for 19-59%, and Tyranitar's Rock Slide is a guaranteed OHKO on Talonflame.

Opponent brings a Drizzle rain core (Pelipper + Swift Swim Mega Swampert/Basculegion) backed by Prankster Whimsicott and Primarina. Serperior is the hard counter to every Water-type, OHKOing Mega Swampert and threatening Basculegion/Primarina after one Contrary boost. Rotom-Wash OHKOs Pelipper with Volt Switch before it can Hurricane, and burns physical Swift Swim sweepers. Incineroar provides Fake Out + Intimidate cycling to disrupt their tempo. Klefki sets dual screens behind Light Clay to blunt rain-boosted attacks; Thunder Wave neutralises Swift Swim speed. Mega Metagross deletes Whimsicott with any Steel move and trades favourably into Primarina. Corviknight offers Tailwind to match their speed tier and a sturdy Flying/Steel pivot that walls non-Water attacks.

Sun team anchored by Charizard Y and Torkoal Drought+Heat Rock. Venusaur's Chlorophyll pushes its Speed past 200 in sun, turning Growth-boosted Giga Drain and Sludge Bomb into an overwhelming sweep. Aegislash is completely immune to Psychic (Ghost typing) and walls Farigiraf and Armarouge for free, while Sacred Sword and King's Rock flinch pressure handle physical threats. Meowscarada's Protean gives STAB on every move, making it a fast mixed revenge killer and cleaner. Skarmory lays Stealth Rock (4× against Mamoswine) and Spikes, provides a Defog-resistant physical wall with Sturdy, and Whirlwinds out setup.

Sun offense anchored by dual Drought setters (Charizard Y and Torkoal) to power Fire moves and unlock Venusaur's Chlorophyll speed. Aegislash is the critical Ghost-type answer to Mega Gengar's Shadow Tag, immune to trapping while threatening Gholdengo with super-effective Shadow Ball. Heracross provides Fighting/Bug coverage with Moxie snowball, demolishing Tyranitar and Excadrill at 4x and 2x respectively, plus Vacuum Wave priority. Skarmory is the physical wall, setting Spikes and using Whirlwind to phaze setup sweepers. Venusaur exploits Chlorophyll speed in sun to spread Sleep Powder (shutting down Gengar's Shadow Tag) while firing instant Solar Beam and Sludge Bomb for coverage.

Klefki sets Prankster screens + Thunder Wave to control Sneasler's speed and blunt Armarouge's special output. Incineroar cycles Intimidate onto Sneasler/Mamoswine while Darkest Lariat threatens Farigiraf. Dragapult (213 Spe) outspeeds and OHKOs Sneasler with Life Orb Psychic Fangs. Clawitzer's Mega Launcher + Expert Belt Aura Sphere and Dark Pulse break Archaludon and Farigiraf. Mega Metagross cleans late-game with Tough Claws-boosted STABs once threats are paralysed or removed. Rotom-Wash spreads burns and pivots with Volt Switch.

Mega Floette is the primary breaker for Dragapult and Incineroar, while Garchomp and Goodra pressure their Steel/Electric core from complementary angles. Talonflame supplies reliable Tailwind, Scrafty disrupts leads with Fake Out and Snarl, and Competitive Milotic punishes Incineroar while checking Gliscor and providing Icy Wind insurance.

Klefki sets Prankster Light Screen/Reflect to neuter Fairy Aura-boosted attacks and protect Dragapult from Mega Alakazam's Shadow Ball. Mega Metagross is the primary breaker — Jolly 178 Speed outruns both Mega Floette and Garchomp, OHKOing the former with Meteor Mash. Dragapult cleans Psychic-types with Life Orb Shadow Ball and nukes Garchomp with Draco Meteor, but needs Tailwind or screens before facing Mega Alakazam. Incineroar provides Intimidate cycling and Fake Out disruption (avoid Parting Shot into Hatterene). Rotom-Wash burns physical threats like Garchomp and pivots with Volt Switch. Corviknight supplies Tailwind, a second Steel/Fairy resist, and Mirror Armor to reflect Scrafty's Intimidate.

This six targets the opponent’s sand and spread-damage core with Mamoswine’s Ground/Ice pressure, Armarouge’s Wide Guard, and Archaludon’s strong special Steel/Dragon attacks. Farigiraf blocks opposing priority and can reverse the speed matchup with Trick Room, while Sneasler and Dedenne provide fast disruption against Mega Gengar, Grimmsnarl, and the slower sand attackers. Flash Fire Armarouge is also a safe pivot into Chandelure, while Thick Fat Mamoswine improves the matchup into Fire- and Ice-based coverage.

The opponent's biggest threat is Unburden Sneasler (base 120, doubled after item pop), which guaranteed-OHKOs Tyranitar with 4x-SE Close Combat. Gholdengo is the perfect counter: immune to both Fighting and Poison STABs while also resisting Archaludon's Dragon/Steel STABs. Sand core (Tyranitar + Excadrill) provides speed control and Rock Slide flinch pressure into Armarouge/Altaria; Excadrill runs High Horsepower over Earthquake to avoid chunking Gholdengo/Tyranitar allies and still threatens possible OHKOs on Archaludon and Sneasler. Mega Gengar at 200 Speed outspeeds the entire roster pre-Unburden and uses Taunt to shut down Farigiraf Trick Room and Sinistcha recovery. Grimmsnarl Prankster screens plus Spirit Break neuters the opponent's special attackers. Tauros-Aqua Intimidate plus Expert Belt delivers possible OHKOs on Mamoswine (Close Combat) and Armarouge (Wave Crash) while softening physical hits team-wide.

The opponent brings a prominent sun core with Mega Charizard Y and Torkoal, alongside Chlorophyll Venusaur and physical threats like Meowscarada and Heracross. We deploy a rain team anchored by Pelipper's Drizzle to override their sun and empower our water attackers. Mega Swampert abuses rain with Swift Swim to dismantle Charizard, Torkoal, and Venusaur, while Basculegion and Primarina clean up defensive walls like Toxapex and Aegislash. Whimsicott provides crucial speed control via Tailwind and Prankster support, and Forretress sets hazards and handles physical attackers.

Opponent is running a rain core with Mega Swampert, Basculegion, and Pelipper backed by Mega Ampharos as a special breaker. My six pivot away from Sun to handle this: Toxapex with Regenerator and Rindo Berry is the primary Water and Ground check, Venusaur Calm-walls special Water/Ghost/Fairy pressure, Aegislash is the dedicated Mega Ampharos and Alakazam switch-in with 202 SpD and Expert Belt-boosted super-effective hits, Skarmory sets dual hazards and Whirlwind-phazes setup, Heracross with Moxie snowballs through Forretress and physical walls, and Protean Meowscarada with Choice Scarf at 190 Speed revenge-kills Alakazam and cleans late game.

The opponent brings a potent sand core in Tyranitar and Excadrill alongside Gholdengo, Grimmsnarl, Mega Gengar, and Paldean Tauros (Aqua). We establish a robust rain team featuring Pelipper, Mega Swampert, Basculegion, Primarina, Whimsicott, and Forretress to flip the weather, outspeed sand rush under rain, and break through their defensive backbones.

We bring a dominant rain team featuring Pelipper, Mega Swampert, and Basculegion-Male, supported by Whimsicott, Primarina, and Mega Ampharos. Every Pokémon follows the Champions format EV caps strictly: exactly 66 total Stat Points per Pokémon, with no single stat exceeding 32 points (distributed across multiple stats like Atk, Def, SpA, SpD, and Spe to avoid hitting >32 in HP, Def, SpA, or Spe).

Cloud Nine Altaria suppresses Pelipper's rain while providing Tailwind, letting the team answer Swift Swim threats without committing to Trick Room. Mamoswine's Freeze-Dry and Archaludon's Thunderbolt pressure the Water core, while Sinistcha redirects attacks and sustains the team; Sneasler supplies Fake Out, Quick Guard, and immediate pressure into Whimsicott, Alakazam, and Forretress. Dedenne adds Nuzzle speed control and Eerie Impulse support against Primarina, Mega Ampharos, and other special attackers.

Use Talonflame/Garchomp to force a fast Tailwind mode, while Scrafty/Hatterene gives a credible Fake Out + Trick Room pivot into Torkoal and slower Water/Steel structures. Mega Floette is the primary cleaner and keeps Energy Ball specifically for Swampert; Milotic is the long-game Palafin and physical-Water answer. Preserve Talonflame’s Sash and Scrafty’s Fake Out pressure to deny opposing Trick Room or create the turn Floette needs to Mega safely.

This six combines Altaria's Cloud Nine and Tailwind with immediate pressure from Mamoswine, Armarouge, and Archaludon, covering weather, Garchomp, Metagross, Floette, Hatterene, and Milotic without depending on Trick Room or Wide Guard. Farigiraf denies opposing priority and Imprisons Trick Room while providing Helping Hand support, and Scarf Sneasler gives a fast answer to Mega Alakazam and Scrafty. Yache Mamoswine and Flash Fire Armarouge improve the Talonflame/Garchomp matchup while the combination of Thunderbolt, Energy Ball, and Grass coverage prevents Milotic from being safely ignored.

Bring both Mega options: Mega Alakazam is the primary anti-Trick Room and Sneasler answer, while Mega Floette is the preferred Tailwind endgame when Steel- and Poison-types are contained. Talonflame plus Scrafty create early tempo with Tailwind, Taunt, Fake Out, and Intimidate; Garchomp pressures Archaludon and Armarouge, while Competitive Milotic punishes Qwilfish Intimidate and can Haze away Stamina boosts. Preserve Floette and Milotic carefully against Mamoswine, and use Alakazam's Taunt rather than priority disruption when Farigiraf is on the field.

Opponent runs a rain core (Pelipper Drizzle + Mega Swampert/Basculegion Swift Swim) with Whimsicott Prankster support and Primarina as a special nuke. Tyranitar's Sand Stream immediately overrides rain, shutting down Swift Swim speed doubling; Excadrill at 280 Spe under Sand Rush outspeeds their entire roster and sweeps with Rock Slide spread + Iron Head for Fairies. Gengar-Mega at 200 Spe traps with Shadow Tag post-Mega and OHKOs Pelipper (Thunderbolt 4x), while Sludge Bomb and Shadow Ball threaten Primarina and Basculegion respectively. Grimmsnarl's Dark typing makes it immune to Whimsicott's Prankster moves, and Prankster Taunt shuts down their setup; dual screens help the frail sweepers survive. Hydrapple resists Water and possibly OHKOs Mega Swampert with 4x SE Giga Drain, pivoting with Regenerator. Gholdengo's Steel/Ghost typing gives it a 4x Ghost resist into Basculegion while Good as Gold blocks all status moves.

Sand core (Tyranitar + Excadrill) provides ultimate speed control—Excadrill at 280 Spe under sand outspeeds Dragapult's 213 and everything else. Tyranitar's Helping Hand (+5 priority) turns Excadrill's High Horsepower into a reliable OHKO on Mega Metagross. Houndoom is the primary wallbreaker: Flamethrower OHKOs Metagross/Klefki/Corviknight, Dark Pulse OHKOs Dragapult, and Flash Fire lets it switch into Incineroar Fire moves aimed at Tyranitar. Mega Gengar traps and removes threats with Shadow Tag—Shadow Ball for Dragapult, Energy Ball as the team's only SE answer to Rotom-Wash, and Taunt to shut down Klefki/Rotom-Wash status. Gholdengo's Good as Gold blocks Prankster TWave and WoW while Shadow Ball hits Metagross SE via Psychic weakness. Tauros provides Intimidate support and Close Combat to remove Incineroar.

Opponent leans on hyper-offensive Megas (Alakazam 150 Spe, Mega Floette 155 SpA) and strong physical threats (Garchomp, Scrafty). Our six answer with three pillars: (1) hazard pressure via Glimmora Stealth Rock/Spikes/Toxic Debris and Skarmory Spikes to wear everything down; (2) priority and speed control — Palafin Hero-form Aqua Jet, Mimikyu and Aegislash Shadow Sneak, plus Skarmory Tailwind to let our whole team outrun 150 Spe; (3) dedicated Fairy and Psychic checks — Mimikyu SD Play Rough deletes Mega Floette and shreds Hatterene, Aegislash's Steel typing tanks Psychic and Fairy STAB while King's Shield cripples physical attackers, and Toxapex Regenerator absorbs Garchomp's Earthquakes and provides a Haze safety net. Win condition is Palafin Flip Turn into Hero form sweeping after hazards stack.

Mega Gengar (130 Spe, 170 SpA, Shadow Tag) is the centerpiece with Grimmsnarl screens + Tyranitar/Excadrill sand. Dragapult outspeeds Gengar and threatens OHKO with Life Orb Shadow Ball. Rotom-Wash walls Excadrill (Iron Head 10-12%) and threatens Hydro Pump KOs on both sand members. Incineroar cycles Intimidate with Fake Out + Parting Shot, Chople Berry lets it eat Tauros-Aqua Close Combat. Mega Metagross Tough Claws Psychic Fangs guarantees OHKO on Gengar; Bullet Punch cleans weakened threats. Klefki matches Grimmsnarl's screens with Light Clay. Serperior snowballs with Contrary Leaf Storm into Tyranitar, Excadrill, and Tauros-Aqua.

This team dismantles the opponent's core of Mega Metagross, Dragapult, and Incineroar through layered offense, sturdy pivoting, and hazard attrition. Palafin and Mimikyu form a potent sweeper pair—Palafin flips into Hero form for devastating Close Combat and Waterfall, while Mimikyu's Disguise plus Focus Sash guarantees a safe Swords Dance or Play Rough hit to destroy Dragapult and Incineroar. Toxapex and Aegislash anchor the defense, walling physical threats with Regenerator recovery and King's Shield attack-drops while punishing with Liquidation burns and Shadow Ball. Glimmora lays Stealth Rock and Spikes with Lum Berry for status protection, and Toxic Debris passively punishes special attackers. Meowscarada's Protean and 192 base Speed let it revenge-kill anything with a guaranteed-STAB move—Flower Trick crits Corviknight, Dark Pulse obliterates Dragapult, Energy Ball OHKOs Rotom-Wash, and Brick Break pressures Mega Metagross.

Rotom-Wash walls Palafin's Jet Punch (0.25x in sun with Water resist) and threatens OHKO with Thunderbolt. Dragapult outspeeds the entire opposing roster and pressures Palafin/Aegislash/Mimikyu with Life Orb coverage. Serperior's Contrary Leaf Storm snowballs while OHKOing Swampert and threatening Palafin. Incineroar cycles Intimidate + Fake Out to neuter Meowscarada and Mimikyu, with Flare Blitz OHKOing Meowscarada. Mega Metagross provides Tough Claws Bullet Punch priority to break Mimikyu's Disguise and clean weakened targets. Gliscor punishes Glimmora's Toxic Spikes via Poison Heal and threatens the Torkoal/Glimmora/Toxapex core with Expert Belt Earthquake.

We bring our dedicated rain core of Pelipper, Mega Swampert, and Basculegion-Male, alongside Whimsicott, Primarina, and Mega Ampharos. Every Pokémon strictly adheres to the Champions format rule: at most 32 points in any single stat and at most 66 total points across the spread. Pelipper sets rain immediately to give Mega Swampert and Basculegion overwhelming Swift Swim speed and power against Incineroar and Mega Metagross, while Mega Ampharos and Primarina pressure defensive pivots like Rotom-Wash and Serperior.

Register both Mega options: Mega Alakazam is the clean immediate answer to Mega Gengar, while Mega Floette is the preferred endgame when Gengar and Gholdengo are contained. Garchomp pressures the revealed sand/Steel core, Talonflame supplies Tailwind and Grimmsnarl disruption, and Scrafty plus Competitive Milotic provide the Intimidate, Snarl, and Icy Wind insurance needed against their alternate physical and special modes.

Same rain matchup we beat 2-0 in Week 1. Serperior is the hard counter to every Water-type, OHKOing Mega Swampert and threatening Basculegion/Primarina after one Contrary boost. Rotom-Wash walls Water attacks (Waterfall 28-47%, Wave Crash 52-77%), OHKOs Pelipper with Volt Switch, and burns physical Swift Swim sweepers. Incineroar provides Fake Out + Intimidate cycling to disrupt their tempo. Klefki sets dual screens behind Light Clay to blunt rain-boosted attacks; Thunder Wave neutralises Swift Swim speed. Mega Metagross deletes Whimsicott with Steel STAB and cleans with Bullet Punch. Corviknight offers Tailwind to match their speed tier and walls Whimsicott completely. Opponent may adapt with Mega Ampharos or Alakazam, but the core plan remains sound — remove Pelipper early, paralyse the Swift Swim sweepers, and let Serperior snowball.

This is a rematch against an opponent who beat me 1-2 in week 1 using Fake Out Scrafty + Mega Floette leads with Garchomp Life Orb EQ as the primary win condition. I bring the Sand core (Tyranitar + Excadrill) for speed control—Excadrill at 140 Spe under sand outspeeds Floette-Mega, Garchomp, and Manectric while Rock Slide threatens Talonflame (4x) and Iron Head threatens Floette (2x). Mega Gengar at 200 Spe outspeeds the entire roster except Alakazam-Mega and can OHKO Floette-Mega with Sludge Bomb (53-109%), Hatterene with Sludge Bomb (62-202%), and Alakazam-Mega with Shadow Ball (64-148%). Gholdengo is the defensive anchor: Steel/Ghost resists Fairy (NVE from Floette's Light of Ruin at 27-87%), immune to Fighting (Scrafty Drain Punch), and resists Psychic (Alakazam-Mega Psychic at 15-46%). Grimmsnarl runs Adamant for Spirit Break OHKO potential on Garchomp (47-102%) and Scrafty through Roseli Berry (52-113%), with Prankster dual screens to keep Tyranitar alive against Garchomp EQ (39-68% under Reflect) and Scrafty Drain Punch (35-66% under Reflect). Rotom provides Levitate Ground immunity to switch into Garchomp EQ freely, Thunderbolt for Talonflame (43-158%) and Milotic (28-89%), Will-O-Wisp to neuter Garchomp/Scrafty/Metagross, and Thunder Wave for speed control on Floette-Mega and Alakazam-Mega.
